title: Making Sense of Mahmoud v. Taylor
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio reads the Supreme Court’s Mahmoud v. Taylor decision, which let parents opt elementary children out of LGBTQ-themed storybook lessons, through the lens of how reading is actually taught. His argument is that the legal reasoning is sound but assumes curriculum means a list of assigned shared texts, whereas many classrooms use the reader’s workshop model with self-selected books from classroom libraries. That raises a question the Court left unanswered, namely whether the opt-out duty is triggered only by whole-class read-alouds or by a book merely sitting on a classroom shelf. He contends that parents will not distinguish assigned from chosen books, because teachers stocked the shelves and the choice happens in instructional time. The mismatch between the public’s content-focused view of curriculum and the ambient view inside schools, he concludes, will keep generating friction and possibly lawsuits.
points: Pondiscio argues that the Supreme Court treated curriculum as a list of assigned books, while much elementary reading instruction runs on student choice from classroom libraries.
The workshop model leaves the ruling’s line between instructional and non-instructional exposure unclear, since read-alouds are only one route by which a book reaches a child.
From a parent’s view a book picked from a classroom shelf during instructional time is not neutral, so the defence that a book was not assigned is weak.
The gap between the public’s content-focused idea of curriculum and the ambient definition used inside schools will keep producing friction and parent complaints.
quotes: But don’t be surprised if Mahmoud proves to be less than the last word. Not because SCOTUS’s legal reasoning is muddled—it’s not—but because of the way reading is taught in many elementary classrooms. The gap between how courts think “curriculum” works and how it’s actually implemented in elementary classrooms is vast. And that means schools will likely keep finding themselves on the receiving end of angry phone calls, and possibly lawsuits, from parents blindsided by what their children bring home in their backpacks.

The line the Court drew seems bright: If schools use contested materials instructionally—especially in ways that make exposure unavoidable—parents have a right to know and a right to say no. Montgomery County’s approach and guidance seems heavy-handed and didactic. But in common practice, the line between “instructional” and “not instructional” is far from clear.

From a judicial perspective, it might matter whether a book is “assigned” and exposure compelled. But from a parent’s perspective, it probably doesn’t. If a first grader comes home with It’s Okay to Be Different or I Am Jazz, parents are unlikely to distinguish between something their child picked up on her own and something their teacher handed them. Nor should we assume that the difference is meaningful.

Most non-educators—including parents, policymakers, and judges—think of “curriculum” as a list of books that every child reads. Something on the syllabus. A shared text. Yet that’s not how ELA works in many classrooms anymore. Although the workshop model has come under fire in recent years, it’s still a common, even dominant approach to elementary reading instruction across the country.

This is where Mahmoud and classroom practice potentially—and predictably—collide. The Court treated the issue as one of compelled exposure. But in an ELA class built on student choice, what counts as “compelled”? If you make available a limited, curated set of books is that choice is free or coerced?

In the final analysis, there is a foreseeable mismatch between the expanded, ambient definition of curriculum inside schools and the traditional, content-focused definition held by the public. The Court didn’t resolve that mismatch. It barely acknowledged it and, indeed, might not be entirely cognizant of it. But it will almost certainly keep generating friction.
